rv.q: The problem is that the fringes of the drama become very busy with the symbolism, which swamps everything else.
This is not, I'm afraid, a vintage Tosca – but Purves's Scarpia just might be.

Disastrously muddled in concept, incoherent and clumsy, pointlessly overviolent for trashy effect (including in a ludicrous “shock” ending), sometimes unintentionally risible and often poorly sung, Annilese Miskimmon’s production is all the more worrying for being created by one of the people who actually runs ENO.
Few stagings have been as vague – if not actually misguided – about when and where the action takes place.
After all, this bold version of Tosca could be viewed as an exhilarating operatic The Spy Who Loved Me : it has a licence to thrill.
And that’s the story of this Tosca, a fine idea overpowered by a stalled and bland set design that leaches its power.
The production is just too unanchored to succeed.
This Tosca is an opera for our time.

There is no doubting the political punch of this Tosca, whose thrust remains true to the spirit and soul of Puccini’s opera.
Ultimately, this is a compelling and emotionally charged Tosca. Miskimmon's reimagining never obscures the essentials of the story.
The pounding, passionate score emerges as the unchallenged victor of the evening.
The staging feels heavy-handed, its visual and dramatic choices insisting on their meaning rather than allowing the drama to speak for itself.
Annilese Miskimmon's new staging is the sixth I've encountered at the Coliseum, and easily the worst.
Miskimmon’s Tosca is an enjoyable and accessible production, complete with spectacular (unspoiled) ‘shocks’, excellent performances and modern commentary.
The standout performance comes from the ENO orchestra under Ben Glassberg, who embody every ounce of the majesty of Puccini's score.

cn.t: ENO's modernized Tosca divides critics sharply. Glassberg's conducting and the orchestra earn widespread praise, but the contemporary staging proves polarizing, with some finding it thrilling while others deem it misconceived and dramatically inert.
